title: The Triliteral Root System & Broken Plurals I
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 6; Ryding Ch. 7)
objectives: Extract the three-consonant root (al-aṣl al-thulāthī) using the ف-ع-ل metric pattern.
Recognize common broken plural patterns (أَفْعَالٌ, فُعُولٌ, فِعَالٌ, فُعُلٌ).
Apply the non-human plural agreement rule (feminine singular modifiers).
recallPrompt: From Chapter 5: How do sound masculine and feminine plurals form their endings?

sections.heading: Roots, Patterns (Awzān), and Broken Plurals
sections.body: Most Arabic nouns and verbs derive from a three-consonant root represented schematically by ف-ع-ل (f-ʿ-l). Instead of adding a suffix, most Arabic nouns form their plural internally by rearranging vowels and adding prefixes or infixes—this is the broken plural (jamʿ al-taksīr), which declines with short vowels like a singular noun.

sections.label: Non-Human Plural Agreement
sections.summary: Any plural referring to non-human objects, animals, or abstract concepts (jamʿ ghayr al-ʿāqil) is grammatically treated as feminine singular for adjective, pronoun, and verb agreement.

sections.irab: الكُتُبُ: مُبْتَدَأٌ مَرْفُوعٌ بِالضَّمَّةِ | جَدِيدَةٌ: خَبَرٌ مَرْفُوعٌ مُفْرَدٌ مُؤَنَّثٌ
sections.notes: الكُتُبُ is a non-human broken plural, so its predicate جَدِيدَةٌ takes the feminine singular form.

sections.heading: Learning Plurals with Singulars
sections.body: Because broken plural patterns vary by noun, always learn each noun together with its plural (e.g., كِتَابٌ / كُتُبٌ, بَيْتٌ / بُيُوتٌ).
